article_text:
Director Peter Berg faced numerous challenges shooting his latest film, “ The Mosquito Bowl .”

Based on Buzz Bissinger’s book, the film tells the true story of four college football stars — Tom Francis as David Schreiner, Nicholas Galitzine as John McLaughry, Ray Nicholson as Tony Butkovich and Bill Skarsgård as Bob Baumann — who are called to serve in the Marines during World War II.

Related Stories

‘Pride and Prejudice’ Trailer: Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden Reboot Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy's Love Story for Netflix

U2 to Play Halftime Show for NFL's Thanksgiving Eve Game in What League Calls 'a New NFL Holiday Tradition'

From football camp to visceral, harrowing sequences of war in the Pacific, the story takes audiences through it all, immersing them in the experience. But one moment completely stumped the director: a scene featuring Tony and an island parrot in the jungle. In Bissinger’s book, Tony sends his parents photos of a parrot perched on his shoulder.

Berg explained, “Buzz writes about it, so we had to get a parrot.” The film was shot on location in Queensland, Australia. “We were in the middle of the woods, and it’s not easy to find a parrot,” Berg shared during a recent Q&A in Hollywood. Joining him were Nicholson, executive producer Ezra Emanuel and producer Alex Gayner. In the conversation, moderated by Variety’s senior artisans editor Jazz Tangcay, Berg said he turned the task of finding a parrot over to Gayner so he could continue shooting the film.

The day before the scene, Berg learned Gayner and the team had found a parrot. “The parrot arrives with four handlers, and they are serious about it … it’s the only parrot on the island,” Berg explained. Fortunately, the bird was trained, and Berg knew it was in good hands. The handlers also made sure no one harmed the parrot.

Berg recalled, “Ray is brought on to set; I’m not allowed to say anything. They’re in charge, and they’re directing Ray and then they bring the parrot out.” He continued, saying he had been assured the parrot had been clipped so it wouldn’t fly away. “Nobody on the crew could talk — dead silence. I’m scared. They put the parrot down. I said, ‘Can we roll?’ They said, ‘No. Let the parrot settle.’”

The director called Nicholson “incredibly professional” for doing everything he needed to do, using hand signals to maintain silence and avoid startling the bird. “As soon as I say ‘Action!’ the fucking parrot flies off. It’s gone. It just flies away into the jungle, into a 100-foot tree,” Berg laughed. His first thought was about the headlines: “It’s going to be ‘Peter Berg kills and loses the parrot.’ So I’m freaking out. This is bad.”

The search for the parrot delayed filming for a few hours until the bird was finally found in a tree and had to be coaxed down. When the handler retrieved the parrot, they tied a friendly string to its leg. “And we got the shot,” Berg said.

“The Mosquito Bowl” is in theaters now and debuts on Netflix Nov. 25.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 工厂之梦：艺术家运营的集体 L’Abominable 在这座传奇法国制片厂的废墟中，为电影实验室想象一个未来
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "当罗伯特·奥特曼决定在巴黎郊外的 Éclair 电影制片厂拍摄《洗衣店》（The Laundromat，1985）时，他已经受够了好莱坞。他对美国制片人感到幻灭（“一切都建立在商业之上，”他对《纽约时报》说），于是远走他乡，来到让·雷诺阿拍摄《大幻影》（1937）、路易斯·布努埃尔执导《朦胧的欲望对象》（1977）的地方——一个长期以来感觉像是电影世界中心的地方。除了雷诺阿和布努埃尔，勒内·克莱尔和科斯塔-加夫拉斯也曾在 Éclair 拍片，动画师埃米尔·科尔在制片厂早年也曾受雇于此。但 Éclair 位于塞纳河畔埃皮奈的河畔园区所做的远不止制作电影。它还制造摄影机，并在其实验室冲洗和印制胶片，处理的 35mm 胶片比法国任何地方都多，包括在公司制片厂之外拍摄的素材。Éclair 制作了吉姆·贾木许的法国发行拷贝，还有阿基·考里斯迈基的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当数字媒体在世纪之交颠覆了电影的命运时，Éclair 的命运也被颠覆了。这些创立于 1907 年的实验室于 2015 年关闭。那一年，公司宣告破产。但如果你今天穿过工厂大门，经过 Éclair 蓝黄相间的闪电标志，你会听到施工的声音。拐进左边那栋 Éclair 称为“Production”的建筑，你会看到一个正在成形中的放映厅，后面有一个珠宝盒般的放映间。走到下一个房间——直到几年前，摄影机底片还在那里的巨型机器中冲洗——你会看到它正在安装小 20 倍的胶片冲洗机——但终究还是冲洗机。当大门明年打开时，这里将成为艺术家运营的电影实验室 L’Abominable 的新家：Navire Argo，令人联想到一艘船，它追求的是白银而非伊阿宋金羊毛的黄金（“argo”是对法语 argent 的戏仿，argent 指使胶片对光敏感的金属）。除了放映厅和实验室，Navire Argo 还将包含存放拷贝、修理设备和教人们如何拍摄、冲洗和放映的空间。它建在电影过去的废墟之上，是一个大胆的宣言：这种媒介拥有未来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不久前，像 Éclair 这样的地方遍布世界各地。有美国的柯达、日本的富士、两个德国的爱克发和 ORWO 这样的胶片制造商。也有像阿莱这样的摄影机制造商和像 DuArt 这样的实验室——这些工厂无形地矗立在我们所谓的电影“产业”背后，连同它的明星和拍摄、市场和首映。Éclair 是这个工业体系中的巨头，而且难得的是它涉足如此之广。电影、实验室、摄影机——它们都曾在这里，在某个时刻。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "L’Abominable 创立于 1996 年，多年来在这个体系的边缘运作。它以格勒诺布尔的 MTK 实验室和伦敦电影制作人合作社等传奇机构为蓝本，信条很简单：光化学胶片的潜力强大且远未耗尽，因此这种媒介的工具和工艺应该向任何想使用它们的人开放。实验室来者不拒，任何有项目的人都可以，只要那个项目是用胶片做的。从它这里诞生的数百部作品中，有 Frédérique Devaux 手工上色、手工冲洗的作品，包括她的 K 系列（2001–2008）；Camilo Restrepo 的短片和他的首部长片《Los conductos》（2020）；以及 Noah Teichner 光学印制的拾得影像随笔《Navigators》（2022）。L’Abominable 主要使用 16mm，而非大多数商业实验室处理的 35mm。它避开了像 Éclair 那样利润优先的做法（尽管奥特曼将其视为逃离好莱坞贪婪的避难所，这家法国制片厂却是靠流行、可复制的配方建立起名声的）。和其他艺术家运营的电影实验室一样，它既致力于使用和教授光化学工艺，也出于必要致力于维护和修理机器，其中许多机器已不再生产；它的艺术家同时也是技师和修补匠。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此，数字转向对 L’Abominable 来说是一笔苦乐参半的意外之财。乔治·卢卡斯在 1999 年的《星球大战前传一：幽灵的威胁》中使用了高清视频，十年后，完全数字化的《阿凡达》上映。到 2012 年，全球最大的胶片制造商柯达已经破产。随着胶片的前景开始黯淡，制造摄影机、冲洗机和放映机的工厂的前景也随之黯淡。生产线停滞，机器被丢弃，公司倒闭或试图调整商业模式以适应数字化的当下。今年夏天与我交谈时，L’Abominable 联合创始人 Nicolas Rey（《Soviets Plus Electricity》，2002；《differently, Molussia》，2012）回忆说，那些年他在废品场和拍卖会上找到印片机和放映机，学习它们如何运作，并把它们修好。2011 年，实验室被逐出它的第一个家——巴黎北郊阿涅尔的一间地下室——之后，这些机器成了附近拉库尔讷沃一个前工业厨房新空间的主力。电影人再也找不到更好的地点了：厨房是化学的领地，实验室恰好落得其所。联合创始人 Pip Chodorov 在 2014 年的《Millennium article_text:
When Robert Altman decided to shoot The Laundromat (1985) at the Éclair film studios outside Paris, he’d had enough of Hollywood. Disillusioned with American producers (“everything’s based on commerce,” he told The New York Times ), he shipped off to the place where Jean Renoir made Grand Illusion (1937) and Luis Buñuel directed That Obscure Object of Desire (1977)—a place that had long felt like the center of the film world. In addition to Renoir and Buñuel, René Clair and Costa-Gavras had made movies at Éclair, and animator Émile Cohl was on the payroll in the studio’s early days. But Éclair’s riverside campus in Épinay-sur-Seine did more than just produce films. It made cameras too, and processed and printed film at its laboratories, which handled more 35mm than anywhere else in France, including footage shot outside the company’s studios. Éclair made Jim Jarmusch’s French release prints, and Aki Kaurismäki’s.

As digital media upended film’s fortunes at the turn of the millennium, Éclair’s fortunes were upended, too. The labs, established in 1907, shuttered in 2015. That year, the company declared bankruptcy. But if you walk through the factory gates today, past Éclair’s blue and yellow lightning-bolt logo, you’ll hear the sounds of construction. Turn into the building on your left, which Éclair called “Production,” and you’ll see a screening room in the making, with a jewel box of a projection booth in the back. Head to the next room, where, until just a few years ago, camera negatives were processed in massive machines, and you’ll see it being fitted with film processors 20 times smaller—but processors all the same. When the gates open next year, this will be the new home of the artist-run film laboratory L’Abominable: the Navire Argo, evoking a ship bent on silver instead of the gold of Jason’s fleece (“argo” is a play on the French argent , for the metal that makes film sensitive to light). In addition to the screening room and the lab, the Navire Argo will contain space to archive prints, repair equipment, and teach people how to film, process, and project. Built in the ruins of film’s past, it’s a bold statement that the medium has a future.

Not long ago, places like Éclair were all over the world. There were film manufacturers like Kodak in America, Fuji in Japan, and Agfa and ORWO in the Germanies. There were also camera makers like Arri and labs like DuArt—factories that stood, invisibly, behind what we call the film “industry,” with its stars and shoots, markets and premieres. Éclair was a giant in this industrial system, and a rarity in that it did so much. The films, the labs, the cameras—all of them were here, at one point or another.

L’Abominable, which was founded in 1996, operated on the outskirts of this system for years. Modeled on the MTK lab in Grenoble and on legendary institutions like the London Film-Makers’ Co-op, it has a simple credo: photochemical film’s potential is powerful and far from exhausted, and so the medium’s tools and processes should be accessible to anyone who wants to use them. The lab takes all comers, anyone with any project, as long as that project is on film. Among the hundreds of titles that have emerged from it are Frédérique Devaux’s hand-colored, hand-processed works, including her K series (2001–2008); Camilo Restrepo’s shorts and his debut feature Los conductos (2020); and Noah Teichner’s optically printed found-footage essay Navigators (2022). L’Abominable works primarily with 16mm, not the 35mm that most commercial laboratories process. It eschews the profits-first approach of places like Éclair (although Altman saw it as a refuge from Hollywood rapacity, the French studio built its name on popular, repeatable formulas). And like other artist-run film laboratories, it is committed as much to using and teaching photochemical processes as it is, by necessity, to maintaining and repairing machines, many of which aren’t made anymore; its artists are also technicians and bricoleurs.

The digital turn was thus a bittersweet windfall for L’Abominable. George Lucas used HD video in 1999’s Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace , and a decade later, the fully digital Avatar was released. By 2012, Kodak, the world’s largest film manufacturer, had gone bankrupt. As film’s prospects began to fade, so did those of the factories making cameras, processors, and projectors. Production lines ground to a halt, machines were discarded, and companies folded or tried to adjust their business models to the digital present. Speaking with me this summer, L’Abominable co-founder Nicolas Rey ( Soviets Plus Electricity , 2002; differently, Molussia , 2012) recalled finding printers and projectors in scrapyards and at auctions in these years, learning how they worked, and fixing them up. In 2011, after the lab was evicted from its first home, a basement in the northern-Paris suburb of Asnières, these machines became the mainstays of a new space in a former industrial kitchen in nearby La Courneuve. The filmmakers couldn’t have asked for a better location: the kitchen is chemistry’s domain, and the lab fell right into place. The drains and vents, co-founder Pip Chodorov wrote in Millennium Film Journal in 2014, were already exactly where they needed to be.

Éclair was still operating at this point. It hung on longer than most of the big laboratories in France, and after its bankruptcy, the city of Épinay-sur-Seine bought the site. When, around 2020, the mayor made the unlikely decision to transform it into a multiuse cultural space—and not more lucrative high-end apartments or corporate properties, as L’Abominable member Emmanuel Falguières ( Nulle part avant , 2018) pointed out in my interview with him and Rey—it was another lucky turn for L’Abominable, which was being forced out of its miraculous kitchen. The filmmakers approached the city council, seeing in Éclair’s “Production” building the home for the Navire Argo, a longstanding dream. In 2022, they were promised a 35-year (in a nod to 35mm) lease on the building, rent-free, as long as they could raise the money to renovate it.

It would be easy to look at the Navire Argo taking shape in what used to be Éclair and see a nose thumbed at an industry to which many artist-run film laboratories emerged as a reaction. Yet as John Powers observes in his 2023 book Technology and the Making of Experimental Film Culture , experimental cinema’s relationship to the commercial film industry isn’t only about opposition. It’s also about connections forged by the technologies that make film possible and malleable, no matter the context or the capital involved. You can see this at work in what’s becoming the Navire Argo. Take the nearly room-sized processors that used to stand in the “Production” building. Three had to be discarded—they’re built for amounts of film beyond what the Navire Argo will ever handle, and the volume of chemicals needed to keep them running would be wastefully large. However, the fourth processor is small enough that L’Abominable filmmakers can make use of it, and will.

Machines like this are the cornerstone on which film-laboratory work has always rested. From cinema’s earliest days, most lab employees learned on the job. Some had backgrounds in chemistry or engineering, and there were some training courses, but you didn’t need a university or technical degree to do the work. For the most part, you needed to know the formulas and techniques, which you repeated across years, or a career. The same is true at L’Abominable, where learning also hinges on technology, as more experienced members of the lab teach novitiates how to use the processors, printers, and cameras. A retired Éclair color grader acknowledged these affinities in 2022, when he accompanied the newspaper Libération through the disused laboratories. He found the experience overwhelming—in his words, “like seeing a woman who’d left me”—but it also felt right to him that L’Abominable would move into the former Éclair. The knowledge that had been abandoned in the early 2000s, left on the curb with the printers and processors, was back where it belonged.

The color grader’s emotion is understandable. Today, few film factories are doing what they used to do. Cameras aren’t made anymore at the former Debrie factory in Paris’s 11th arrondissement; there’s a convenience store on the ground floor. In Binghamton, New York, you can rent a light-filled loft in the old Ansco camera plant, whose facade still proudly bears the company’s name. The same is true of Kodak’s Berlin factory, which has also been transformed into luxury apartments, surrounded by streets still named things like An der Filmfabrik (At the Film Factory) and Am Filmlager (At the Film Warehouse). The future Navire Argo is an exception. Under L’Abominable’s watch, a section of the Éclair laboratories is not only returning to its original function, but also assuming some of the multipurpose identity that made Éclair so central to the film industry in the first place. Part of this has to do with the machines that L’Abominable has amassed over the years, which already allow it to accommodate a film’s entire postproduction workflow, up to the release print and laser subtitling. When the Navire Argo is finished, its work will extend to photochemical film’s projected and archival lives.

It’s an exciting position to be in for the filmmakers, but also a precarious one. There are the finances, for one thing. Since it is open to all, the lab is organized as a nonprofit; most of its funding comes from state sources, and those aren’t guaranteed. L’Abominable has partly crowdfunded the money to build the Navire Argo, and they still need donations. Beyond this is the fragile ecosystem in which all film laboratories operate—not just artist-run ones. Because this ecosystem depends on film, it also depends on Kodak, which still makes the vast majority of the world’s motion-picture stock. The existence of film laboratories has always been inextricably tied to the fortunes, and whims, of film manufacturers. In the 1920s, Kodak attempted to buttress its monopoly by buying up U.S. laboratories, supplying them exclusively with its film, and threatening independent laboratories with unwinnable competition if they tried to buy from any other company. When a 1954 antitrust suit forced Kodak to make its processing formulas public, Powers writes, the number of independent labs in the country grew fivefold.

For filmmakers today, however, the question isn’t which company’s film to use. It’s whether to use film at all, which makes things even more uncertain. The big directors with their massive productions, like the Nolans and the Tarantinos, help keep Kodak in business and laboratories running. So do archives: in the U.S., a significant amount of lab work comes from agencies like the National Film Preservation Foundation, which is committed to restoration and preservation on film (more stable, over the long term, than digital formats). In France, the L’Abominable filmmakers are part of an effort to have photochemical film practice—all of its parts, from making film to projecting it—recognized by UNESCO as a form of intangible cultural heritage.

If the Navire Argo allows us to divine a future for film, these last two efforts might be key. Preserving films, and preserving the practice itself, are reasons enough to keep making celluloid. Yet an industry built on these pillars wouldn’t look like what brought Robert Altman to Eclair 40 years ago. Untethered from commercial cinema’s logics of volume and profit, this industry may be smaller, less vulnerable to shifts in the market, and as a result, more sustainable. L’Abominable would be happy with that. In its manifesto for the Navire Argo, the lab emphasizes that the project is about “knowledge and possibilities.” L’Abominable has been imagining these possibilities for 30 years, and in the Navire Argo, they’ll be imagined all over again in another 35. Thirty-five years is a long time, but that’s the point. The film factory is dead. Long live the film factory.

The author thanks Thomas Aschenbach, Emmanuel Falguières, Gary Griffin, Nicolas Rey, and Vincent Terlizzi for interviews and conversations crucial to this article.

article_text:
Stand-up comedians have always had a reverence for what they like to call a “comic’s comic” — a fellow comedian who works with such distilled purity and edge, diving head-first into the gnarly metaphysics of comedy, that the comics end up worshipping him more than the public does. (He’s the stand-up-comedy equivalent of an ultimate cool indie-rock cult band.) Gilbert Gottfried was a comic’s comic. So are Larry David and Doug Stanhope and Maria Bamford. And Norm Macdonald was one too, except that as you watch Judd Apatow ’s juicy and haunting documentary “ Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald ,” you realize that there was a special thing about him. He was a comic’s comic…who everyone else loved too.

As the movie demonstrates, Macdonald’s credentials as a comic’s comic were unassailable. We see his very first network television appearance on May 9, 1990, on “Late Night with David Letterman,” where he did a bit about the devil commanding someone to kill his family and chop them into bits and stuff the pieces into a duffel bag. (Then the killer learns that the devil is a friend who was kidding.) He speaks in that familiar halting deadpan; he already knows how to draw the audience into his head.

Popular on Variety

On “Saturday Night Live,” where Macdonald, starting in 1993, spent four seasons as one of the all-time great hosts of Weekend Update, he returned, over and over, with a bluntly obsessive fixation that couldn’t be denied, to the subject of O.J. Simpson, and to the fact that Simpson had murdered his wife. Why was this funny? Because every time Macdonald made a joke of it, his assertion of O.J.’s guilt was a way of tapping back into the shocking unreality of it. His every O.J. joke had the effect of a giddy slap. He would not relent, and that wound up getting him fired from “Saturday Night Live” (Don Ohlmeyer, the president of NBC’s West Coast division who was responsible for axing Macdonald, was O.J. Simpson’s best friend). Now that’s a comic’s comic thing to do.

On “SNL,” and in his legendary litany of late-night talk-show appearances, and in his stand-up routines, Norm Macdonald had an oxymoronic quality — a slightly disconnected aggression, where he would zero in on a topic, and a joke, that he knew would be prickly, and that might take him “over the line,” but he couldn’t help himself. He had to say the naughty thing, to blurt out the forbidden. Telling that joke would be a catharsis; it would be comedy. Not telling it would be defeat.

At times, he had a streak of Andy Kaufman’s antisocial hostility, as if comedy was his way of testing both himself and the audience, seeing what they would accept, and seeing if they would accept him . A strange thing that emerges in “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald” is that Macdonald was a compulsive liar, in both his stand-up act and his life, the two planes of existence sometimes entwined around the same deception. That’s part of why he always seemed a bit of a space cadet. You could never really tell whether he meant what he was saying. We learn that he never went to high school…and also that he did (and graduated when he was 14)…that he never went to college…but actually did as well. On the eve of the pandemic, he described himself to an audience as “a young 68” (he was 60 at the time). He also describes himself, to Larry King, as “deeply closeted,” and when King asks if that means he’s coming out as gay, he says no, he’s straight…and then indicates that claiming to be straight is an expression of how closeted he is. You can hear Andy Kaufman chortling in his theater-of-the-absurd heaven.

Yet the thing about Norm Macdonald is that he executed all this with a smiling charm and a winsome agreeability that made him irresistible to a wide swath of fans. He wasn’t a prickly punk — more like a transgressive Teddy bear. In the early days, including the “SNL” years that made him famous, he was quite handsome, with a lean face and twinkly eyes and dimples and a coif of curly hair and a killer grin that made him look like the slightly goofy cousin of Paul Newman. Fifteen years before Norm Macdonald, Chevy Chase had been the first break-out superstar of “Saturday Night Live,” transforming his own Weekend Update quizzicality into big-screen celebrity, and he accomplished this not because he was a great actor but because he had a sublime detachment coupled with tall preppie good looks that he used ironically. His handsomeness was part of the joke, as well as the cushion for it.

Macdonald, though, didn’t use his looks in that way; they just kind of existed alongside the bratty edge of his comedy. And so when he was booted from “SNL,” he acted like he’d been kicked off a cliff. He was still out there in the culture, but he floundered around, and this, as the documentary captures, was related to his strange and slippery personality: his compulsive sincerity (which meant that he didn’t quite know how to package himself), his compulsive put-ons (which meant that he was actually scared to show who he was), his compulsive insecurity (which meant that he didn’t truly believe in himself as a star), mixed with an element of self-sabotage (his way of confirming all those anxieties about himself).

After all of that, “Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald” is rooted in what a beloved comedian Norm MacDonald was, and still is. In the opening montage, several people, like Howard Stern, reference the rabbit hole you can get into just by going onto YouTube and watching clips of Macdonald on late-night talk shows. He had countless appearances that were gems, because he always invested his talk-show time with a spark of danger. He couldn’t just be a straight shooter, but he had to make his put-ons feel real. At times, he was as philosophical as Lenny Bruce — but Bruce talked about religion only to mock it, whereas Macdonald, at one point, reveals that he’s a Christian who’s a true believer. (This is a man who would introduce his sidekick as someone who jerked off punks for $15 under a bridge.) It’s all part of his mystery.

The movie is spanked along by clips of Letterman, Jerry Seinfeld, Conan O’Brien, and Dave Chappelle, and Apatow, working with the editor Jake Hostetter, assembles the comedy snippets in an entrancing way, so that we feel the underground sprawl of Macdonald’s career. He could be a great impressionist (his Bob Dole on “SNL” may have helped turn the 1996 presidential election; his Quentin Tarantino was inspired). He kept doing stand-up, but didn’t require the comedy stage to be great; just talking to Jane Fonda on his video podcast, “Norm Macdonald Live,” he was insanely funny. We see his appearance change quite a bit over the years, as he evolves into a puffier version of himself, something that happened in part because he spent his last nine years secretly fighting leukemia. (He died in 2021.) Yet the audience stayed with him — at least, more than the entertainment industry did.

Macdonald wasn’t the first “incorrect” comedian to run afoul of the comedy police, but it felt like he was the first such comic of a certain day and age (namely, ours). He should have had his own late-night talk show, but when he learned that he was up for one — and that he had been passed over for the yuppie dullard Craig Kilborn — that was a sign that his comedy was ruffling feathers. At the same time, he cultivated incorrectness in a way that could be mindless. When he went on “The View” and said that Bill Clinton was guilty of “murder,” he claimed that he was just doing a bit, but since the “bit” fed into right-wing conspiracy theory, it seemed like an episode of sour derangement. And when he defended Roseanne Barr, after her racist tweet in 2018, he did it out of loyalty (one of his first gigs was as a writer for “Roseanne”) but in a tone-deaf way, as if what she’d said in her tweet was some trivial joke. (It was not; it was egregious.) All of this fed into the perfect shitstorm that was The Decline of Norm Macdonald.

We pretend that comedy is just fun, a means to an end — the end being to make you laugh. But the few who are chosen to be “comic’s comics” occupy that rarefied stratosphere because they know that comedy is more than laughter, and that laughter is more than we give it credit for. You laugh for a lot of reasons, but one of those reasons can be when an idea goes off in your head like a small explosion. That’s why comedy can tickle your soul, snap you back to life, cleanse you. And that’s the kind of comedian Norm Macdonald was. He had a devilish gleam, but he provoked a laughter that sparked you and lifted you up, landing you on the side of the angels.

‘Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald’ Review: Judd Apatow’s Juicy and Haunting Portrait of a Comedy Star as Troubled as He Was Hilarious

article_text:
Clayface premiered at the Hollywood Legion Theater in Los Angeles, where its stars reunited for the big event.

Tom Rhys Harries plays the title role in the DC Comics film, which also stars Naomi Ackie and Max Minghella.

The film also includes Eddie Marsan, David Dencik, Nancy Carroll, Joshua James, Francesca Corney, Ruby Sear, and Wil Coban.

RELATED: ‘Matchbox: The Movie’ Red Carpet Premiere Photos: John Cena, Jessica Biel, Teyonah Parris & More

Per DC, the film “unravels one man’s horrifying descent from rising Hollywood star to revenge-filled monster in a story that explores the loss of one’s identity and humanity, corrosive love, and the dark underbelly of scientific ambition.”

Mike Flanagan and Hossein Amini penned the script for the pic, produced by Reeves, Lynn Harris, and DC Studios’ James Gunn and Safran. Executive producers are Michael E. Uslan, Chantal Nong Vo, Lars P. Winther, Rafi Crohn, and Paul Richie.

RELATED: Luca Guadagnino’s ‘Artificial’ Red Carpet Premiere Photos: Andrew Garfield, Jason Schwartzman, Billie Lourd, Ike Barinholtz & More

At Comic-Con , director James Watkins teased that Clayface was going to give people a lot of ick and a lot of gore,” adding, “But there’s also an emotional core that gives it a dimension. When you sit and watch this, and you feel the anima of an audience responding to the film, there’s some comfort in that, I suppose.”

editorial_excerpt_zh: “这里将有影像颗粒与目光的种子、音乐、奇特的工艺、LUX 巡展，当然还有茶点吧和本地餐饮。”Zone i 的创始人莫妮卡·桑托斯（Monica Santos）和马特·雅各布（Mat Jacob）此前曾这样宣布，而他们也兑现了诺言。不仅如此，还有：相遇、辩论、在……中畅游

"translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着奥克西唐语复调合唱团 ABAL 的首场排练声响起，远处地平线上很快传来了雾笛的回应。营地里响起了集结号：“大家去谷仓集合，摄影即兴创作会（Photo Jam regards”（种子与目光的颗粒），该地区的五位摄影师应邀在方丹磨坊及其河岸上以空白委托（carte blanche）的形式分享他们的一系列作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "摄影师安妮·皮耶居（Anne Piégu）在其系列作品《普通建筑的故事》（Récit d'architecture ordinaire）中，展示了一个正在消逝的乡村世界的痕迹，以及那些曾生活于其中的人们的故事。我们遇到了杰奎琳（Jacqueline），她 22 岁时结婚并随丈夫来到家庭农场。她负责挤牛奶。还有 60 年前带着女儿们来到这里的科莱特（Colette）。她是第一个在一个小山谷里建房的人，正对着一个有着酿酒传统的村庄的酒窖。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "通过这些故事，安妮讲述了塑造她童年的风景和生活方式的变迁。她的目光超越了乡村世界，因为各地领土都在变化，风景在转移，某些生活方式正在消逝。留下来的唯有摄影，它是唯一能够保存那些不复存在之物的痕迹的媒介。贝诺·勒隆（Beno Lelong）通过《关于一座不复存在的城市的笔记》（Notes sur une ville qui n'existe "paragraph", "text": "有时摄影本身成为了需要去寻找的痕迹。今年，一些展览将那些被时间掩盖的目光重新唤回。首先是让-皮埃尔（Jean-Pierre）的目光，通过由塞巴·拉勒曼（Séba Lallemand）呈现的系列作品《让-皮埃尔、拐杖与漂亮人们》（Jean-Pierre, Béquilles et Beautiful People）。塞巴在 2000 年代初为一家机构执行委派任务时，在巴黎遇到了无家可归的让-皮埃尔。他们谈论了摄影，让-皮埃尔坦白了自己想尝试这种媒介的愿望，于是塞巴把装好胶卷的奥林巴斯 MJU-II 相机递给了他。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随后是一段奇特的交往。塞巴冲洗了这些照片，他们约定“在香榭丽舍大街富凯餐厅（Fouquet's）对面的一张长椅上见面，那是他的大本营”，然后塞巴把冲好的照片拿给他看。在刺眼的闪光灯光下，让-皮埃尔捕捉到了富人区、上流社会及其盛装、奢华与浮华的一面。他还捕捉到了街道、人行道、苦难以及那些我们每天路过却从未真正端详的面孔。“人们看着他这个流浪汉，而他看着人们：富人、迷失的夜游神、穷人。”让-皮埃尔沉迷于此，甚至给自己买了一些小型柯达一次性相机。“令人难以置信的是，他对摄影的着迷程度不亚于他对酒精的依赖。”", "Blind Magazine", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在 Zone i 展示的精选作品选自 47 卷胶卷。不会再有第 48 卷了，因为让-皮埃尔在此之前已经离世。塞巴形容让-皮埃尔“有着天国般的巴黎流浪汉外表，骄傲、醉醺醺的，塌鼻子，头发油腻”。在展出的唯一一张他的照片中，他半闭着眼睛，被阳光刺得睁不开眼，头发蓬乱，嘴唇上叼着香烟，脖子上戴着一条闪闪发光的链子（肯定是个假货）。关于他的身份，人们一无所知：“他对自己的过去守口如瓶。”留下的唯有他的目光，它将数百万人的日常生活升华了。这是一份免于审判的见证，也是用柯达快照对人文主义街头摄影的最后一次调侃式回击。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在磨坊的顶楼，第二位摄影师从阁楼的尘埃中被重新发掘出来。克里斯蒂安·路易斯（Christian Louis）在出版了14本书后便被人遗忘，他的作品在去世后重新进入人们的视野。这些作品展现了一种介于纪实与诗意叙事之间的摄影风格，它追寻的不是事件本身，而是事件发生之侧、现实缝隙中的印记。在明暗对照中，他捕捉到了正处于变革中的法国所经历的阵痛，介于工业衰退、城市扩张与新兴生活方式之间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "画框之外", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "田野中央响起了一声“咔哒”声。那是托马斯·奥祖（Thomas Ozoux）的机具“光影照相机”（Photocotype）：“一台老式复印机，我给它加装了一个放大镜镜头，并用一个旧衣柜的面板将它包裹起来。”它高高矗立在 Zone i 迷秀的中心，这是一件由大约100扇旧门和回收镜子组成的艺术品。自童年起，托马斯就对自己的胶片进行“折磨”，并对相机进行改装。他继续用自己的发明扭曲现实。他的长时间曝光让人联想起达盖尔银版摄影法，而他的“失败之作”与“畸变之作”则展现了现实的另一面。他的光影照相机作品也在方丹磨坊（Moulin de la Fontaine）展出。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在迷宫的出口处，又一声“咔哒”声响起。这一次是一支气枪。拍完肖像之后，还有什么比向一张肖像开枪更好呢？这正是马特·雅各布（Mat Jacob）的射击摊所提供的，该摊位被朴素地命名为《无辜的狗屁照片》（Innocent Crappy Photos）。这是对那些经常出现在公众舆论法庭面前、同样饱受技术暴力摧残的影像的一种致敬。开火！", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/thomas-ozouux-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Thomas Ozouux", "credit": "Blind Magazine", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/christian-louis-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Christian Louis", "credit": "Blind Magazine", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为了给这一切恢复平静，没有什么比带着一张记录你自身脉搏的摄影作品来抚慰心灵更有效的了。这项体验由 Trigone 团队的实验室提供，作为 Lux 网络的成员，该团队在摄影诞生200周年之际将他们的房车停在了 Zone i。通过将心脏跳动的电脉冲与感光表面上光子的运动进行对话，这里的摄影过程将一个人的心脏转化成了图像。这些装置都在提醒我们，Zone i 绝不仅仅是一个节日，它首先是一种感官体验，并体现了该地方由马特·雅各布所表达的坚定决心：“让摄影焕发生机，无论它是严肃的还是轻松的。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "点击此处了解关于 Zone i 的更多信息。", "links": [{"text": "More information on Zone i here.", "url": "https://www.zone-i.org/"}], "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“There will be grain and seeds of gazes, music, strange processes, the LUX Tour and of course, the refreshment bar and local catering.” Monica Santos and Mat Jacob, the founders of Zone i, had announced it, and they kept their word. There was more: encounters, debate, swims in the river and live music."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As the first rehearsals of ABAL, a choir of Occitan polyphonic songs, ring out, a foghorn soon answers from the horizon. A rallying call goes out across the grounds: “Meet in the barn, the Photo Jam Session is about to start!” For the third year running, the Photo Jam Sessions invite photographers of all backgrounds and ages to present their work as a short projection. “The original idea was to evolve the portfolio review, where you find yourself face to face with maestros who assess your work,” explains Mat Jacob. The aim is to restore a form of horizontality with an audience, and to spark emulation, debate, advice and remarks. Mat Jacob sums it up simply: “It can be very enriching to be criticized with kindness.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/dsf0752-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Zone i © Séléné Brault", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/dsf0465-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Zone i © Séléné Brault", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While some projects are already far along, accomplished or even finished, most are still in progress or being shown to an audience for the first time. Practices intersect: documentary photography, experiments, video, editing or more singular technical processes. From Jean Puybaraud’s work on the genocide of the Yaghan people to Eve Campestrini’s series exploring the imaginary of a collective of farmers committed to the ecological transition, the subjects differ, but the social and environmental concerns echo each other."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Questioning the territory"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "From May to October, Zone i deploys a multidisciplinary program of exhibitions, talks, workshops, concerts and artistic projects around image, environment and education. The festival found refuge nearly ten years ago at the Moulin de la Fontaine, a former place of production and gatherings that is now a cultural laboratory dedicated to photography. Just as the miller once worked grain with the force of water, photographers now shape the grain of images there, capturing light, time and the stories of the living world. With “Graines et grain de regards” (Seeds and Grain of Gazes), five photographers from the area are invited to share one of their series as a carte blanche, in the Moulin de la Fontaine and along its banks."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In her series “Récit d’architecture ordinaire” (Tale of Ordinary Architecture), photographer Anne Piégu shows the traces of a rural world that is disappearing, along with the stories of those who lived in it. We meet Jacqueline, who married at 22 and joined her husband on the family farm. She was the one who milked the cows. And Colette, who arrived with her daughters 60 years ago. She was the first to have a house built in a small valley, facing the cellars of a village with a winemaking tradition."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/anne-piegu-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Anne Piegu", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/eric-zeziola-683x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Eric Zeziola", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Through these stories, Anne recounts the transformation of the landscapes and ways of life that shaped her childhood. Her gaze goes beyond the rural world, because everywhere territories are changing, landscapes are shifting and certain ways of living are vanishing. What remains is photography, the only medium able to preserve the traces of what no longer exists. Beno Lelong bears witness to this with “Notes sur une ville qui n’existe plus” (Notes on a City That No Longer Exists). For several years, the artist roamed Nantes, living in squats and empty houses among other places. His images archive the remnants of an alternative city, the city of his memories, and also of a way of life that has since disappeared."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Between tribute and legacy"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sometimes photographs themselves become traces to be found. This year, some of the exhibitions bring back gazes that time had covered over. The first is Jean-Pierre’s, through the series “Jean-Pierre, Béquilles et Beautiful People” (Jean-Pierre, Crutches and Beautiful People), presented by Séba Lallemand. Jean-Pierre was homeless in Paris when Séba met him in the early 2000s, while working on a commission for an agency. They talked about photography, Jean-Pierre confessed his wish to try the medium, and Séba handed him his loaded Olympus MJU-II."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A curious trade followed. Séba developed the images, they arranged to meet “on a bench opposite the Fouquet’s on the Champs-Elysées, his headquarters,” and Séba showed him the prints. In the harsh light of the flash, Jean-Pierre captured the wealthy districts, the jet set and its share of pomp, luxury and glitter. He also captured the street, the pavement, the misery and those faces we pass every day without really looking at them. “People looked at him, the tramp, and he looked at people, the rich, the lost night owls, the poor.” Jean-Pierre got so caught up in the game that he bought himself small disposable Kodaks. “What was incredible is that he was as hooked on photography as he was on alcohol.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/seba-lalemand-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Seba Lalemand", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/beno-lelong-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Beno Lelong", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/seba-lalemand-2-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Seba Lalemand", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The selection presented at Zone i is drawn from 47 rolls of film. There would be no 48th, as Jean-Pierre died before. Séba describes Jean-Pierre as having “the appearance of the celestial Parisian tramp, proud, drunk, with a smashed nose and greasy hair.” In the only image of him on show, he appears with eyes half closed, blinded by the sun, hair disheveled and cigarette hanging from his lips, a bling-bling chain (surely fake) around his neck. Of his identity, nothing is known: “he stayed very discreet about his past.” All that remains is his gaze, which transfigures the daily life of millions of people. A testimony free of judgment and a last thumbing of the nose at humanist street photography, with a Kodak snap."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "On the top floor of the mill, a second photographer is pulled from the dust of the attic. Forgotten after publishing 14 books, Christian Louis sees his work rediscovered after his death. It reveals a photography halfway between documentary and poetic narrative, one that seeks not the event but what happens beside it, in the interstices of reality. In chiaroscuro, he captures the jolts of a France in the midst of change, between industrial decline, urban expansion and new ways of life."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Out of frame"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A “clack” rings out in the middle of the field. It is the machine of Thomas Ozoux, the Photocotype: “an old photocopier to which I added a magnifying glass lens and that I covered with the panels of an old wardrobe.” It sits enthroned at the center of the Zone i labyrinth, a work made of around 100 old doors and recycled mirrors. Since childhood, Thomas has tortured his films and tinkered with his cameras. He continues to bend reality with his inventions. His long exposures recall those of the daguerreotype, while his “failures” and “monsters” reveal another side of reality. His photocotypes are also on show at the Moulin de la Fontaine."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the exit of the labyrinth, another “clack” rings out. This time it is an air rifle. article_text:
“There will be grain and seeds of gazes, music, strange processes, the LUX Tour and of course, the refreshment bar and local catering.” Monica Santos and Mat Jacob, the founders of Zone i, had announced it, and they kept their word. There was more: encounters, debate, swims in the river and live music.

As the first rehearsals of ABAL, a choir of Occitan polyphonic songs, ring out, a foghorn soon answers from the horizon. A rallying call goes out across the grounds: “Meet in the barn, the Photo Jam Session is about to start!” For the third year running, the Photo Jam Sessions invite photographers of all backgrounds and ages to present their work as a short projection. “The original idea was to evolve the portfolio review, where you find yourself face to face with maestros who assess your work,” explains Mat Jacob. The aim is to restore a form of horizontality with an audience, and to spark emulation, debate, advice and remarks. Mat Jacob sums it up simply: “It can be very enriching to be criticized with kindness.”

While some projects are already far along, accomplished or even finished, most are still in progress or being shown to an audience for the first time. Practices intersect: documentary photography, experiments, video, editing or more singular technical processes. From Jean Puybaraud’s work on the genocide of the Yaghan people to Eve Campestrini’s series exploring the imaginary of a collective of farmers committed to the ecological transition, the subjects differ, but the social and environmental concerns echo each other.

Questioning the territory

From May to October, Zone i deploys a multidisciplinary program of exhibitions, talks, workshops, concerts and artistic projects around image, environment and education. The festival found refuge nearly ten years ago at the Moulin de la Fontaine, a former place of production and gatherings that is now a cultural laboratory dedicated to photography. Just as the miller once worked grain with the force of water, photographers now shape the grain of images there, capturing light, time and the stories of the living world. With “Graines et grain de regards” (Seeds and Grain of Gazes), five photographers from the area are invited to share one of their series as a carte blanche, in the Moulin de la Fontaine and along its banks.

In her series “Récit d’architecture ordinaire” (Tale of Ordinary Architecture), photographer Anne Piégu shows the traces of a rural world that is disappearing, along with the stories of those who lived in it. We meet Jacqueline, who married at 22 and joined her husband on the family farm. She was the one who milked the cows. And Colette, who arrived with her daughters 60 years ago. She was the first to have a house built in a small valley, facing the cellars of a village with a winemaking tradition.

Through these stories, Anne recounts the transformation of the landscapes and ways of life that shaped her childhood. Her gaze goes beyond the rural world, because everywhere territories are changing, landscapes are shifting and certain ways of living are vanishing. What remains is photography, the only medium able to preserve the traces of what no longer exists. Beno Lelong bears witness to this with “Notes sur une ville qui n’existe plus” (Notes on a City That No Longer Exists). For several years, the artist roamed Nantes, living in squats and empty houses among other places. His images archive the remnants of an alternative city, the city of his memories, and also of a way of life that has since disappeared.

Between tribute and legacy

Sometimes photographs themselves become traces to be found. This year, some of the exhibitions bring back gazes that time had covered over. The first is Jean-Pierre’s, through the series “Jean-Pierre, Béquilles et Beautiful People” (Jean-Pierre, Crutches and Beautiful People), presented by Séba Lallemand. Jean-Pierre was homeless in Paris when Séba met him in the early 2000s, while working on a commission for an agency. They talked about photography, Jean-Pierre confessed his wish to try the medium, and Séba handed him his loaded Olympus MJU-II.

A curious trade followed. Séba developed the images, they arranged to meet “on a bench opposite the Fouquet’s on the Champs-Elysées, his headquarters,” and Séba showed him the prints. In the harsh light of the flash, Jean-Pierre captured the wealthy districts, the jet set and its share of pomp, luxury and glitter. He also captured the street, the pavement, the misery and those faces we pass every day without really looking at them. “People looked at him, the tramp, and he looked at people, the rich, the lost night owls, the poor.” Jean-Pierre got so caught up in the game that he bought himself small disposable Kodaks. “What was incredible is that he was as hooked on photography as he was on alcohol.”

The selection presented at Zone i is drawn from 47 rolls of film. There would be no 48th, as Jean-Pierre died before. Séba describes Jean-Pierre as having “the appearance of the celestial Parisian tramp, proud, drunk, with a smashed nose and greasy hair.” In the only image of him on show, he appears with eyes half closed, blinded by the sun, hair disheveled and cigarette hanging from his lips, a bling-bling chain (surely fake) around his neck. Of his identity, nothing is known: “he stayed very discreet about his past.” All that remains is his gaze, which transfigures the daily life of millions of people. A testimony free of judgment and a last thumbing of the nose at humanist street photography, with a Kodak snap.

On the top floor of the mill, a second photographer is pulled from the dust of the attic. Forgotten after publishing 14 books, Christian Louis sees his work rediscovered after his death. It reveals a photography halfway between documentary and poetic narrative, one that seeks not the event but what happens beside it, in the interstices of reality. In chiaroscuro, he captures the jolts of a France in the midst of change, between industrial decline, urban expansion and new ways of life.

Out of frame

A “clack” rings out in the middle of the field. It is the machine of Thomas Ozoux, the Photocotype: “an old photocopier to which I added a magnifying glass lens and that I covered with the panels of an old wardrobe.” It sits enthroned at the center of the Zone i labyrinth, a work made of around 100 old doors and recycled mirrors. Since childhood, Thomas has tortured his films and tinkered with his cameras. He continues to bend reality with his inventions. His long exposures recall those of the daguerreotype, while his “failures” and “monsters” reveal another side of reality. His photocotypes are also on show at the Moulin de la Fontaine.

At the exit of the labyrinth, another “clack” rings out. This time it is an air rifle. After having your portrait taken, what better than to take a shot at a portrait? That is what Mat Jacob’s shooting stand offers, soberly titled “Innocentes photos de merde” (Innocent Crappy Photos). A tribute to the images that regularly appear before the court of public opinion and suffer, too, the violence of technology. Fire!

And to restore some calm to all this, nothing beats soothing your heart by leaving with the photograph of one of your own pulses. The experience is made possible by the laboratory of the Trigone team, a member of the Lux network, which parks its caravan at Zone i for the bicentenary of photography. By bringing the electrical pulse of a heartbeat into dialogue with the movement of photons on a sensitive surface, the photographic process here transfigures one’s own heart into an image. These devices all remind us that Zone i remains above all a sensory experience, more than just a festival, and reflect the place’s determination, voiced by Mat Jacob: “to bring photography to life, whether it’s serious or not.”

article_text:
U.S. artist and documentarian Lynne Sachs has often screened her past films at Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival , but she’s finally made it in person this year, serving on the First Lights jury, which evaluates docu debuts.

Sachs says she’s been impressed by Ji.hlava films that span the globe while showcasing the full range of filmmaking approaches and perspectives.

“There are about 24 movies to see. It’s kind of revelatory. Already I’ve seen two films here, one from Argentina and one from Congo and they really couldn’t be more different. They make you think about the documentary paradigm.”

Related Stories

Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart

A case in point, she says: “Positionality.” Whose perspective is an audience seeing and is the filmmaker’s role visible or even known?

It’s something Sachs has made crystal clear in her newest film, “Every Contact Leaves a Trace,” screening at Ji.hlava in its Czech premiere.

Sachs herself is clearly onscreen, investigating, making connections, doubting herself, and occasionally seeking help from a youthful niece and nephew as she goes through old business cards, some decades old, wondering at who gave them to her and what traces of lives contacting hers can still remain.

The film is a kind of detective story that eventually enlists the actual analyses of forensic investigators as Sachs follows leads to track down people whose names remain in her box of hundreds of carefully preserved business cards – a good number she admits have lost all meaning to her.

“I actually hired a detective at one point,” she confesses.

Some left burning impressions on her and she has always wondered what became of the card giver – such as an artist whose work touched her years ago or a fellow artist filmmaker who was later canceled over allegations of impropriety.

One card was from a Syrian woman whose family discouraged her from sitting for an on camera to share her experiences as a refugee – so Sachs settles for filming a tribute to the woman’s cooking skills.

Sachs says she is also uneasy about terms that have come into common use for people in docus. Rather than say “protagonists” or “characters,” she much prefers “on camera participants.” Or maybe “visible collaborators who are the people in front of the camera.”

“We’re offered the chance to tell our story by the person behind the camera. What I don’t know is, who is the person behind the camera?”

In the case of “Every Contact,” it’s clear to all who is filming and inquiring as Sachs visibly, sometimes awkwardly, tracks down people who once met her but certainly never expected her to appear again at their doorstep with a camera. It’s a role she has not always put onscreen so clearly, she says.

“I’m trying to reconstruct a life story of life experience from the interactions I’ve had with people…people who left a mark.”

Since the film came out, Sachs says, people have offered her their own collections of old business cards.

“I say, ‘Oh, no!’ This combination of cards only goes back to one person. You’re the person who had that dentist. You’re the person who met that psychoanalyst. Or potential friend on a bus.”

As Sachs investigation progressed, she says, “I was most drawn to the cards that presented the biggest obstacles.”

Some card donors may be impossible to find now. And others presented a different challenge: At times figures from your past have made lasting impressions – but that doesn’t always mean that was mutual.

The process of recounting past encounters is one fraught with traps, says Sachs, as human minds tend to re-enact them in the mind, often editing, sometimes finding specific moments deeply burned in. As Sachs enlists the help of family on her quest, one suggests that it’s not usually even up to us to choose which memories will stay with us and which we’ll lose.

Sachs discovered through her docu detective work that sometimes she did not need to fly across time zones to track down someone she once knew who might not even remember her or feel they shared an important interaction, she says.

“I don’t need to prove I did or didn’t,” says Sachs. “I need to deal with the residue.”
